title: Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface
summary: The first capstone joins chapters 6, 12 and 14 into one polished tool: a read-only memory inspector for **programs you built yourself**, with a Dear ImGui interface showing the region map, a hex view with typed overlays, snapshots with change highlighting, and the telemetry channel from chapter 12. This lesson gives the specification, an architecture, the milestones in order, the acceptance tests and stretch goals.
markdown:
## What you are building **Xenon Inspector** is a desktop tool for looking inside your own running programs while you develop them: Delve, the practice targets of lesson 9.10, and anything else you compile. It answers questions like "what does this struct look like in memory right now?", "which bytes changed when I picked up that item?" and "how is this program's address space laid out?". The ground rules from chapter 12 are part of the specification, not an afterthought: > [!important] Scope > - The inspector only opens processes whose executable lies under a folder you configure as your **build output** (for example `D:\dev\bin`), or processes it starts itself from there. It refuses anything else, with a message explaining why. > - It is **read-only**: it never writes to the target's memory. > - It uses documented APIs only (`OpenProcess` with `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ`, `VirtualQueryEx`, `ReadProcessMemory`, the Tool Help snapshot functions) and needs no administrator rights. ## Features | Panel | Shows | Built in | |---|---|---| | **Process picker** | Running processes under the build folder, with a Launch button for executables there | 6.07, 12.01 | | **Region map** | Every region: base, size, state, protection, type, and the module it belongs to; filters and sorting | 6.04, 14.04 | | **Hex view** | Bytes of a selected address range, 16 per row with ASCII; Go to address; follows a pointer on double-click | 12.02 | | **Typed overlay** | A struct definition (from a small text file) laid over the hex view, showing each field's name, type and value | 2.06, 9.09 | | **Snapshots** | Take a snapshot of a range, take another later, and list and highlight the changed ranges | the practice task | | **Telemetry** | If the target publishes chapter 12's telemetry channel, its live values in a table | 12.04, 12.05 | | **Settings** | Build folder, refresh rate, window layout, persisted | 14.05 | ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB UI["ImGui panels
(picker, regions, hex, overlay, snapshots, telemetry)"] --> M["Inspector model
selected process, ranges, snapshots"] M --> P["Process access layer
scope check, OpenProcess, VirtualQueryEx,
ReadProcessMemory, module list"] M --> T["Struct definition parser"] M --> D["Snapshot diff"] M --> C["Telemetry reader (chapter 12)"] P --> W[("Windows APIs")] ``` Keep the layers separate, as lesson 17.01 recommends: the struct parser and the snapshot diff are pure functions with unit tests; the process access layer is the only code that calls Windows; the panels only draw the model and send it commands. Then most of the program can be tested without a target running. ## Milestones Build it in order; each milestone is usable on its own. 1. **Skeleton**: the ImGui window from lesson 14.02 with an empty dock space, a settings file and the build-folder setting. 2. **Process access**: list processes, apply the scope check (resolve the executable path with `QueryFullProcessImageNameW`, then check it is under the build folder after normalising both), open with the minimum rights. Unit-test the path check with lesson 17.04's lessons about `..` and case. 3. **Region map**: the `VirtualQueryEx` walk from lesson 6.04 on the target, shown in a sortable table with module names. 4. **Hex view**: read on demand only the visible rows, handle unreadable pages (`ReadProcessMemory` fails or reads partially: show `??`), and refresh at the configured rate. 5. **Snapshots and diff**: copy a range, compare later, list changed ranges, highlight them in the hex view. 6. **Typed overlay**: parse definitions such as `struct Player { i32 health; f32 x; f32 y; u8 flags; }` with natural alignment (lesson 2.05) and show the values. 7. **Telemetry**: connect to the target's telemetry channel if it exists, and show its version check from lesson 12.06. 8. **Hardening**: lesson 12.07's checklist: the target exiting at any moment, huge regions, invalid addresses typed by the user, and a fuzz test of the struct parser (17.03). ## Acceptance tests The inspector is done when: - it refuses a process outside the build folder, including one reached by a path with `..`, a different case, or a short 8.3 name; - it shows Delve's region map and its main module's base matches the one Delve prints (lesson 6.09); - the overlay of Delve's `Player` struct shows the health dropping when a monster hits; - a snapshot diff around the inventory shows exactly the bytes that change when an item is picked up; - closing Delve while the inspector is reading it gives a clear message, not a crash; - the unit tests pass under AddressSanitizer; - it never opens a handle with write or operation rights (verify with Process Explorer's handle view). ## Stretch goals - Read the target's PDB with the DIA SDK or `dbghelp` to show real type names and fields instead of hand-written definitions. - A "watch list" of addresses with a plot of each value over time (lesson 14.04). - Export a snapshot and its overlay as a report for a bug ticket. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Reading huge ranges every frame > Read only what is visible, and only at the refresh rate. > [!warning] Mixing Windows calls into the UI code > It makes the inspector untestable and the UI slow when a read blocks. > [!warning] Loosening the scope check "just for testing" > The rule is the feature. Keep test targets in the build folder. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What are the inspector's scope rules? - Any process on the machine, read and write, run as administrator + Only processes from your build folder, read-only, minimum rights - Only processes with a window, with full access so values can be changed - Any game the user owns, using whatever technique works > Keeping the tool to your own builds and read-only access keeps it safe and within the course's ground rules. It also uses documented APIs only and never needs administrator rights. ? How is the inspector structured so it can be tested? - All code in the panels, tested by clicking through every window - One large `main` function, tested by running the tool on a real game + Tested pure logic, one Windows access layer, and drawing-only panels - Each panel calls Windows directly, so each can be tested on its own > Pure logic can be tested without any process to read, which is why it is kept away from Windows calls. ? How should the hex view handle a page that cannot be read? - Stop reading and show an error dialog - Show zeros for the unreadable bytes - Retry until the read succeeds + Show `??` for those bytes and keep working > Zeros would look like real data; `ReadProcessMemory` may fail or read only part of a range, so the view must cope. ? Why is the process scope check done on the full executable path after normalising it? + So `..`, case or short names cannot evade it - Because process names are always unique - To make it faster > The same lessons as safe path joining. ? Why read only the visible rows of the hex view? - `ReadProcessMemory` can only read 16 bytes + Reading large ranges every frame is slow - The target would crash > Read what you show. ? Which access rights does the inspector need? - `PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS` - `PROCESS_VM_WRITE` and `PROCESS_VM_OPERATION` + `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION` and `PROCESS_VM_READ` > The least rights for a read-only tool. ```
ideas:
- Complete milestones 1 to 4, then use the region map to find Delve's heap regions while it loads a level.
- Complete the snapshot milestone and use it to find where Delve keeps the player's gold.
- Write the acceptance tests as a checklist in the project's README and tick them off.

cards.q: What are the inspector's scope rules?
cards.a:
Only processes from your build folder, read-only, minimum rights

Keeping the tool to your own builds and read-only access keeps it safe and within the course's ground rules. It also uses documented APIs only and never needs administrator rights.

cards.q: How is the inspector structured so it can be tested?
cards.a:
Tested pure logic, one Windows access layer, and drawing-only panels

Pure logic can be tested without any process to read, which is why it is kept away from Windows calls.

cards.q: How should the hex view handle a page that cannot be read?
cards.a:
Show `??` for those bytes and keep working

Zeros would look like real data; `ReadProcessMemory` may fail or read only part of a range, so the view must cope.

cards.q: Why is the process scope check done on the full executable path after normalising it?
cards.a:
So `..`, case or short names cannot evade it

The same lessons as safe path joining.

cards.q: Why read only the visible rows of the hex view?
cards.a:
Reading large ranges every frame is slow

Read what you show.

cards.a:
`PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION` and `PROCESS_VM_READ`
